books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, Democracy in America by Alexis de Tocqueville

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835, 1840)

stimulus.text: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835): “Amongst the novel objects that attracted my attention during my stay in the United States, nothing struck me more forcibly than the general equality of conditions.” In a later volume (1840) he wrote: “Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions, constantly form associations. They have not only commercial and manufacturing companies, in which all take part, but associations of a thousand other kinds — religious, moral, serious, futile, extensive, or restricted, enormous or diminutive.”
stimulus.source_note: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1 (1835) and vol. 2 (1840), Henry Reeve translation. Verbatim quotations verified against the Project Gutenberg text (eBook 815).

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Tocqueville calls the “general equality of conditions” the fundamental fact of American society because it

options.text: shaped public opinion, laws, and the ordinary practices of life
made all Americans equally wealthy in money and land
options.misconception: Tocqueville writes about equality of conditions, not equal wealth; the gap between rich and poor was widening.

options.text: ended slavery in the Southern states at once
options.misconception: Slavery grew with cotton in the South; equality of conditions did not extend to enslaved people.

options.text: gave women the right to vote in elections
options.misconception: Women could not vote; equality of conditions did not extend to them either.

rationales.A: Tocqueville writes that equality of conditions “creates opinions, engenders sentiments, suggests the ordinary practices of life.” It is the fact from which all his other observations are derived.
rationales.B: Equality of conditions is about social standing, not money. The rich grew richer in this period while the poor crowded into cities.
rationales.C: Slavery was growing, not ending, as cotton spread. Tocqueville's equality did not reach enslaved people.
rationales.D: Women had no vote in this period. Equality of conditions was an equality among free white men.
rationales.general:
1. Read his claim. Equality of conditions is the fundamental fact from which all others seem to be derived.
2. Ask what it touches. He says it shapes opinions, laws, and the ordinary practices of life.
3. Keep its reach straight. It explains American society, but it did not make people equal in wealth.
Background: Tocqueville visited the United States in 1831 with Gustave de Beaumont to study prisons, and his book appeared in 1835 and 1840.
Remember: a writer's fundamental fact is the one everything else hangs from.
